prompt.context: BCG has been hired after 9/11 to look into quantifying the amount of damage to revenue streams that has occurred in the Manhattan hotel business.
prompt.question: How would you go about determining/quantifying the impact of 9/11 on Manhattan hotel revenues, and how would you structure a recovery plan?

clarifying_info.q: Is there a standard metric the hotel industry uses to measure revenue performance?
clarifying_info.a: Hotels use a metric called 'Revpar' which equals average daily room rate multiplied by occupancy rate. Revpar was $200 before 9/11, $125 for the remainder of 2001, $150 for 2002, and $175 for 2003.

clarifying_info.q: What should we assume Revpar would have been if 9/11 had not occurred?
clarifying_info.a: Assume Revpar would have remained flat at $200 for the entire time period.

clarifying_info.q: How many hotel rooms are there in Manhattan?
clarifying_info.a: There are 100,000 hotel rooms in Manhattan.

framework: Segment the market by customer type: US business travelers, international business travelers, and leisure/tourist travelers
Quantify the revenue impact by comparing actual Revpar to the pre-9/11 baseline Revpar across the affected periods
Identify which customer segments suffered the largest losses and why (safety perception, airport delays, etc.)
Develop a targeted recovery plan addressing the root causes for the most impactful customer segments (marketing, promotions, government lobbying, etc.)

questions.prompt: Quantify the total revenue impact of 9/11 on Manhattan hotels across 2001 (post-9/11), 2002, and 2003.
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for Revpar data and number of rooms, then calculate the Revpar shortfall per period multiplied by 100,000 rooms and the number of days in each period. Assume 9/11 occurred mid-September 2001, leaving approximately 110 days remaining in 2001 (mid-Sep to Dec 31).

math.setup: Revpar shortfall = ($200 baseline - actual Revpar) x 100,000 rooms x number of days in period
math.answer: Approximately $3.56 billion in lost revenue across the three periods

questions.prompt: Structure a recovery plan for Manhattan hotels.
questions.guidance: A strong answer segments customers by type, values each segment, identifies which segments declined most, diagnoses root causes (e.g., safety perception for tourists, airport delays/hassle for business travelers), and proposes solutions targeting those root causes — such as marketing campaigns, pricing promotions, or lobbying government for measures that ease travel.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the primary categories of hotel customers and the main reasons each may have reduced travel to Manhattan after 9/11?

categories.name: US Business Travelers
ideas: Fear of flying following the attacks
Perception of New York as a target city
Corporate travel freezes and budget cuts
Preference for video conferencing over in-person meetings

categories.name: International Business Travelers
ideas: Heightened airport security and long delays make travel less efficient
Reduced appetite for US travel among certain nationalities

categories.name: Leisure/Tourist Travelers
ideas: Safety and security concerns about visiting New York
Media coverage reinforcing perception of danger
Discretionary budget cuts during economic downturn post-9/11

recommendation: The revenue impact is approximately $3.56 billion over the post-9/11 period through end of 2003, driven by a Revpar decline from $200 to as low as $125

A recovery plan should prioritize the highest-value segments (likely US business and international business travelers) and address root causes: safety perception, airport friction, and corporate travel reluctance
risks: Recovery may be asymmetric across segments — tourists may return faster than business travelers if corporate budgets remain constrained
Macro factors (additional security incidents, economic recession) outside hotel operators' control could delay recovery
Aggressive discounting to drive occupancy may permanently reset price expectations downward
next_steps: Conduct customer research to quantify the relative size and Revpar contribution of each traveler segment before and after 9/11
Identify which root causes are addressable through hotel-level actions vs. government/industry lobbying
Design targeted marketing and promotional campaigns for highest-priority segments, and engage NYC tourism bodies and government on broader safety messaging and travel facilitation measures
